name: Homburg hat

lead: The Homburg is a felt hat, usually black or grey, with a single lengthwise dent in the crown, a wide grosgrain band and a flat brim curled up at the edges and bound with ribbon. It is traditionally worn with dark lounge suits, dinner jackets and overcoats.

For appearance it works as a finishing accessory: it gives a formal, vintage silhouette and frames the face. It was popularised by Edward VII and later associated with figures such as Anthony Eden, Dwight Eisenhower and the 1972 film The Godfather.

paras: Wearers pair it with tailoring in dark or neutral colors, traditionally a lounge suit or a dinner jacket with an overcoat. Colors are usually black, grey or midnight blue in fur felt. The hat is a styling choice rather than a treatment, so its effect is immediate and ends when it is taken off.

No health risks are documented beyond ordinary hat concerns such as heat. It is uncommon in modern everyday dress, which means it can draw attention, and wearers note the style depends on matching the formality of the outfit.

angle.text: The hat completes a suit-and-overcoat outfit and frames the face with a defined brim and crown. Wearers use it for a classic, formal look.

lead: The Homburg is a semi-formal men's felt hat, usually black or grey, with a single dent down the crown, a wide silk grosgrain band and a flat brim curled into a pencil-roll and edged with ribbon.[1] It takes its name from Bad Homburg in Hesse, Germany.[1]

As a way of improving appearance, it is a classic tailoring accessory: it adds a formal, structured finish to a suit and overcoat. Edward VII, then Prince of Wales, brought the style to Britain, and it later became associated with Anthony Eden, Winston Churchill, Dwight Eisenhower, who wore a black one at his 1953 inauguration, and Al Pacino's grey hat in The Godfather.[1]
Everyday use largely faded from Western men's dress in the 1960s, though some Orthodox Jewish rabbis still wear black Homburgs.[1] No studies have examined the hat.

paras: The Homburg has a gutter crown with a central dent, a flat brim curled upward at the sides, a ribbon-bound brim edge and a wide grosgrain hatband.[1] According to Grokipedia, it is typically made from high-quality fur felt such as beaver or rabbit, and has a softer structure than a bowler.[2]

The hat originated as hunting headwear in Bad Homburg; Edward VII, as Prince of Wales, popularised it in Britain as a less formal alternative to the top hat.[1] Grokipedia places the first commercial production in the early 1880s with the Möckel hat factory, citing a local newspaper report of August 1882 that the Prince had ordered one; that account is AI-generated and unverified.[2]

Anthony Eden made the black version fashionable in the 1930s, giving it the name Eden hat. Eisenhower wore a black Homburg at his 1953 inauguration and Al Pacino's grey one in The Godfather (1972) revived interest.[1]
It remains associated with traditional tailoring and is typically paired with dinner jackets and black lounge suits, though it is worn with other lounge suits as well.[1]
